summary.text: Exact divisibility is obtained by expressing the numerator’s prime valuation as \(\sum_{i\ge1}\lfloor n/p^i\rfloor^2\) and the denominator’s as \(\sum_{i\ge1}\sum_{k=1}^n k\lfloor\lfloor n/p^i\rfloor/k\rfloor\), then bounding each inner sum by the corresponding square. If \(p\nmid t+1\), adding \(t+1\) contributes no \(p\)-factor to either the new gcd row and column or the changed factorial terms, so the quotient’s valuation is unchanged; induction applies this to the successive integers after \(np\), all before the next multiple of \(p\).

full_proof.text:
Let
\[
N(m)=\prod_{1\le j\le m}\prod_{1\le k\le m}\gcd(j,k)
\]
and
\[
D(m)=\prod_{1\le k\le m}\left(\left\lfloor\frac{m}{k}\right\rfloor !\right)^k.
\]
Thus the sequence in question is
\[
a(m)=\frac{N(m)}{D(m)}.
\]
We will first prove that this quotient is an integer. We then prove the key local assertion that, for any prime \(p\), the \(p\)-adic valuation of \(a(m)\) does not change when one passes from \(m=t\) to \(m=t+1\), provided \(p\nmid t+1\). The conjecture follows immediately by iterating that assertion over the numbers strictly between two consecutive multiples of \(p\).

Throughout, for a positive integer \(x\), write \(v_p(x)=\operatorname{ord}_p(x)\) for the exponent of the prime \(p\) in \(x\).

## 1. Valuation of the numerator

Fix a prime \(p\). For positive integers \(j,k\),
\[
v_p(\gcd(j,k))=\min(v_p(j),v_p(k)).
\]
Equivalently,
\[
v_p(\gcd(j,k))
 =\sum_{i\ge 1}\mathbf 1_{p^i\mid j\text{ and }p^i\mid k},
\]
because the summand is \(1\) precisely for
\(i=1,\ldots,\min(v_p(j),v_p(k))\). All these sums are finite.

Using additivity of valuations over products and interchanging finite sums gives
\[
\begin{aligned}
v_p(N(m))
&=\sum_{1\le j,k\le m}v_p(\gcd(j,k))\\
&=\sum_{i\ge1}\#\{(j,k):1\le j,k\le m,\ p^i\mid j,\ p^i\mid k\}.
\end{aligned}
\]
There are exactly \(\lfloor m/p^i\rfloor\) multiples of \(p^i\) between \(1\) and \(m\). Hence
\[
\boxed{
 v_p(N(m))=\sum_{i\ge1}\left\lfloor\frac{m}{p^i}\right\rfloor^2.
}
\tag{1}
\]
Only indices with \(p^i\le m\) contribute.

## 2. Valuation of the denominator

Legendre’s formula states that for every nonnegative integer \(q\),
\[
v_p(q!)=\sum_{i\ge1}\left\lfloor\frac{q}{p^i}\right\rfloor.
\]
Therefore
\[
\begin{aligned}
v_p(D(m))
&=\sum_{k=1}^m k\,v_p\!\left(\left\lfloor\frac{m}{k}\right\rfloor!\right)\\
&=\sum_{k=1}^m k\sum_{i\ge1}
 \left\lfloor\frac{\lfloor m/k\rfloor}{p^i}\right\rfloor.
\end{aligned}
\]
For positive integers \(k,p^i\), successive integer division satisfies
\[
\left\lfloor\frac{\lfloor m/k\rfloor}{p^i}\right\rfloor
 =\left\lfloor\frac{m}{kp^i}\right\rfloor
 =\left\lfloor\frac{\lfloor m/p^i\rfloor}{k}\right\rfloor.
\]
Interchanging the finite sums and putting
\(M_i=\lfloor m/p^i\rfloor\), we obtain
\[
\boxed{
 v_p(D(m))
 =\sum_{i\ge1}\sum_{k=1}^m k\left\lfloor\frac{M_i}{k}\right\rfloor.
}
\tag{2}
\]

We compare each inner sum in (2) with the corresponding term in (1). More generally, if \(0\le M\le m\), then
\[
\sum_{k=1}^m k\left\lfloor\frac{M}{k}\right\rfloor\le M^2.
\tag{3}
\]
Indeed, the terms with \(k>M\) vanish. For \(1\le k\le M\),
\[
k\left\lfloor\frac{M}{k}\right\rfloor\le M.
\]
There are \(M\) such indices, so their sum is at most \(M\cdot M=M^2\), proving (3).

Applying (3) to every \(M_i=\lfloor m/p^i\rfloor\), equations (1) and (2) yield
\[
v_p(D(m))\le v_p(N(m))
\]
for every prime \(p\). Both \(N(m)\) and \(D(m)\) are positive integers. By unique prime factorization, the valuation inequalities for all primes imply
\[
D(m)\mid N(m).
\]
Consequently \(a(m)=N(m)/D(m)\) is an integer, and for every prime \(p\),
\[
\boxed{
 v_p(a(m))=v_p(N(m))-v_p(D(m)).
}
\tag{4}
\]

## 3. Local invariance of the numerator

We now establish the central local result. Fix a prime \(p\) and an integer \(t\ge0\), and suppose
\[
p\nmid t+1.
\tag{5}
\]
We claim first that
\[
v_p(N(t+1))=v_p(N(t)).
\tag{6}
\]

When the indexing square \(1\le j,k\le t\) is enlarged to
\(1\le j,k\le t+1\), all old factors remain unchanged. Every new factor lies either in the new row \(j=t+1\), in the new column \(k=t+1\), or at their common corner. Each such factor has the form
\[
\gcd(t+1,x)\quad\text{or}\quad\gcd(x,t+1)
\]
for some \(1\le x\le t+1\). Every such gcd divides \(t+1\). Under assumption (5), none is divisible by \(p\), and hence every new gcd has \(p\)-adic valuation zero. Additivity of valuations over the product therefore gives (6).

## 4. Local invariance of the denominator

Under the same assumption (5), we next prove
\[
v_p(D(t+1))=v_p(D(t)).
\tag{7}
\]

Consider first an index \(k\) with \(1\le k\le t\). On increasing the numerator in the quotient from \(t\) to \(t+1\), the integer quotient changes according to
\[
\left\lfloor\frac{t+1}{k}\right\rfloor
=\begin{cases}
\left\lfloor\dfrac{t}{k}\right\rfloor+1,&k\mid t+1,\\[4pt]
\left\lfloor\dfrac{t}{k}\right\rfloor,&k\nmid t+1.
\end{cases}
\tag{8}
\]
If \(k\nmid t+1\), the factorial occurring in the \(k\)-th denominator factor is unchanged.

Suppose instead that \(k\mid t+1\). Put
\[
q=\left\lfloor\frac{t}{k}\right\rfloor.
\]
Then (8) says
\[
q+1=\frac{t+1}{k}.
\]
The new factorial is therefore
\[
(q+1)!=(q+1)q!.
\]
Moreover, \(q+1\) divides \(t+1\). If \(p\mid q+1\), then \(p\mid t+1=k(q+1)\), contrary to (5). Thus
\[
v_p(q+1)=0,
\]
and consequently
\[
v_p((q+1)!)=v_p(q!).
\]
Raising these factorials to the \(k\)-th power multiplies both valuations by \(k\), so the \(k\)-th denominator factor has the same \(p\)-adic valuation before and after the increment.

This handles every old index \(1\le k\le t\). There is one additional index, namely \(k=t+1\), in \(D(t+1)\). Its factor is
\[
\left(\left\lfloor\frac{t+1}{t+1}\right\rfloor!\right)^{t+1}
=(1!)^{t+1}=1,
\]
which has valuation zero. Summing the valuations of all denominator factors proves (7).

Combining (4), (6), and (7), we have proved the local invariance statement
\[
\boxed{
 p\nmid t+1\quad\Longrightarrow\quad v_p(a(t+1))=v_p(a(t)).
}
\tag{9}
\]

## 5. Iteration across a block of length \(p\)

Let now \(n\) be a positive integer, let \(p\) be prime, and let
\(k\) satisfy \(0\le k<p\). We prove
\[
v_p(a(np+k))=v_p(a(np)).
\]

For each integer \(r\) with \(1\le r\le k\), one has
\[
p\nmid np+r.
\tag{10}
\]
Indeed, \(p\mid np\). If \(p\mid np+r\) as well, subtraction would give \(p\mid r\). But a positive multiple of \(p\) is at least \(p\), whereas \(1\le r\le k<p\), a contradiction.

Apply (9) successively with
\[
t=np,\ np+1,\ldots,\ np+k-1.
\]
At the step from \(np+r-1\) to \(np+r\), condition (10) is exactly the needed assertion that \(p\nmid t+1\). Hence
\[
\begin{aligned}
v_p(a(np))
&=v_p(a(np+1))\\
&=v_p(a(np+2))\\
&\ \vdots\\
&=v_p(a(np+k)).
\end{aligned}
\]
Since this holds for every \(k<p\), all the values
\[
v_p(a(np)),\ v_p(a(np+1)),\ldots,v_p(a(np+p-1))
\]
are equal. This is precisely conjecture C for A129365.
